name: Tyler Technologies, Inc.
moat_justification: Dominant U.S. state/local govtech franchise: mission-critical systems of record (courts, public safety, tax, finance, schools), ~98% client retention, 87-88% recurring revenue, 12-24 month implementations and state-by-state regulatory logic embedded in the product make switching rare and painful. Measured ROIC proxy is only 4.3-8.8% over the last five fiscal years (rising every year since 2021), which understates the franchise: the invested-capital denominator carries goodwill/intangibles from 50+ acquisitions including the ~$2.3B NIC deal, and the SaaS conversion depressed margins mid-transition — gross margin has recovered from 42.4% (2022) to 46.5% (FY2025) and 47.2% TTM as SaaS mix rises. That written reason is why a 7 stands despite ROIC not yet sitting well above the cost of capital.
fragility_flags: STALE_FY: latest fiscal year ended 10 months ago — check TTM/quarterly OE and consider --base-oe-ps override
NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE: net income and operating cash flow differ by >40% in 2023, 2024, 2025 — find the one-off (tax deposits, impairments, WC swings) before trusting the OE base
one_liner: High-quality govtech compounder, moat 7/10, but at $360.87 it does not clear 15% — weighted IRR 8.3%, weighted IV@15% $157.25; it would need to fall to ~$157 to clear the 15% hurdle.
moat_for: Mission-critical systems of record for courts, public safety, tax assessment, municipal finance and schools — switching means re-implementing core government operations
~98% client retention and 87.8% recurring revenue (FY2025); contracts are long and rarely re-bid
State-by-state regulatory and workflow logic built from the ground up for government, vs generic ERP adapted by Oracle/SAP/Workday
Breadth across 50 states plus the NIC payments platform monetizing the installed base (~500M transactions/yr)
SaaS conversion tailwind: SaaS revenue +21.7% in Q2 2026, 22 straight quarters of >=20% SaaS growth, gross margin expanding with mix
moat_against: Measured ROIC proxy only 4.3-8.8% over the last five fiscal years — pricing power has not yet converted into high returns on the acquisition-heavy capital base
AI lowers the cost of building software, which over time erodes the switching-cost moat of legacy vertical vendors; government buyers are actively evaluating AI budget share
Growth has decelerated to high-single digits (Q2 2026 revenue +8.2%); one-off contract losses happen (Texas payments contract termination drags transaction growth)
Competition from CentralSquare, Motorola Solutions and horizontal platforms (Oracle, Workday, Microsoft) with far larger R&D budgets
Customer budgets are municipal/state appropriations — long sales cycles and budget timing can defer bookings (2025 bookings slump)
